results.title: Martin Scorsese Says Seth Rogen and the Sony Hack “Ruined” His CLEOPATRA Movie With Angelina Jolie
results.description: Martin Scorsese nearly made a Cleopatra movie starring Angelina Jolie, and according to the legendary filmmaker, we can blame Seth Rogen and the infamous Sony hack for killing it. During the first episode of Tribeca's original series Crafty, Scorsese opened up about the abandoned project and how the fallout from Rogen's controversial 2014 comedy The Interview derailed his plans. “We were gonna do Cleopatra at one point, and then they made fun of [Kim Jong Un], and he got mad and blew up everybody at Columbia,” Scorsese said. “Seth Rogen, right? And then he got mad, and [it] ruined Cleopatra.” For anyone who needs a refresher, The Interview starred Rogen and James Franco in a comedy about two Americans recruited to assassinate North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In November 2014, Sony Pictures was hit by a massive cyberattack carried out by hackers who wanted to prevent the film's release. The attack exposed thousands of private emails, internal documents, and embarrassing conversations between Hollywood executives. Among the leaked messages were emails from producer Scott Rudin to then-Sony executive Amy Pascal, including one in which Rudin described Jolie as “a minimally talented spoiled brat.” The resulting controversy created a massive headache for Sony, and Scorsese says his planned Cleopatra film became one of the casualties. “We were gonna do it,” Scorsese also said. “Angelina Jolie. We were going. She was gonna be Cleopatra VII. It was gonna be really wild.” The film was being developed with a screenplay by Eric Roth, who later wrote Scorsese's 2023 crime drama Killers of the Flower Moon. The movie was part romance epic and part “political thriller with assassinations and sex,” according to the movie’s original screenwriter Brian Helgeland. He said: “It had elements of a political thriller with assassinations and sex, but it’s an epic that’s divided between her love affairs with Caesar and Marc Antony. Lots of true events surprised me when I was writing it.” While Rogen obviously wasn't personally responsible for canceling Cleopatra, Scorsese's recollection makes it sound like the Sony hack brought an abrupt end to a project that was moving forward. Scorsese spent his career exploring powerful, complicated people, and it's easy to imagine a fascinating historical epic that could have been unlike the usual Hollywood treatment of the Egyptian ruler. Unfortunately, we'll probably never know exactly what Scorsese had planned. Still, it's crazy to think that a comedy about assassinating Kim Jong Un may have helped prevent Martin Scorsese and Angelina Jolie from bringing Cleopatra to the big screen.

results.title: US election: The key races that could tip control of Congress
results.description: Tuesday’s midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress or Democrats gain the ability to slow President Donald Trump’s agenda during the final two years of his term (and cause other headaches for President Trump). The numbers are straightforward: Democrats need a net gain of three House seats to reach the 218-seat majority threshold. In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53–47 advantage. Democrats need four net gains to reach 51, as a 50–50 split would leave Republicans in control through Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote. Senate: The Republican seats Democrats need to flip North Carolina and Maine are central to the Democratic path. In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper faces Republican Michael Whatley for retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis’s seat. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson. Collins’s ability to attract crossover voters is especially important in a state Kamala Harris carried in 2024. Ohio and Texas could provide decisive gains. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio’s special election. In Texas, Republican Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a closely watched contest after defeating incumbent John Cornyn in the primary. Both races test whether Democrats can win statewide in territory that has favored Republicans. Alaska, Iowa and Kansas provide additional routes. Republican Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola in Alaska; Republican Ashley Hinson faces Democrat Josh Turek for Iowa’s open seat; and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton in Kansas. These contests give Democrats alternatives if they fall short elsewhere. Democrats must also protect their own seats Michigan is a critical defense, with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed facing Republican Mike Rogers for retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters’s seat. In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff faces Republican Mike Collins. New Hampshire’s open Democratic seat features Chris Pappas against Republican John E. Sununu. Every Democratic loss raises the hurdle. Losing one current seat would require Democrats to flip five Republican seats to reach 51. House: Pennsylvania could make the difference Pennsylvania offers three closely watched Republican-held targets: 7th District: Ryan Mackenzie vs. Democrat Bob Brooks. 8th District: Rob Bresnahan vs. Democrat Paige Cognetti. 10th District: Scott Perry vs. Democrat Janelle Stelson. All three Republican incumbents won narrowly in 2024. Democratic victories in these districts alone, with every other seat unchanged, would be enough to flip the House. Other important Republican-held battlegrounds include Michigan’s 7th, Wisconsin’s 3rd, Iowa’s 1st and 3rd, New York’s 17th, Virginia’s 2nd and Arizona’s 6th. With such a narrow majority, individual district results could decide who controls the speaker’s gavel. What it means for markets Republican control of both chambers would preserve Trump’s clearest path to advancing legislation. A Democratic House would force more negotiation over spending and major policy changes. Democratic control of the Senate would also give the party greater influence over appointments and confirmations. For traders, the election is a catalyst for reassessing taxes, spending, regulation and borrowing. The size of the majorities will matter alongside which party wins: narrow control could leave Washington struggling to turn campaign promises into policy.
